unit.unitOverview:
Hello! My name is Rami, and I love buildings. I go to Ehel Academy with my friends Amal, Karim and Nadia. We are a little building team. In this unit, you and your team will build something too!

Do these activities with a grown-up. You can talk, draw, tick and colour. There are no marks. Just have fun and do your best.

outcomes.text: 4. Ask your team: a little survey

explainers.title: 1. What makes a good team?
explainers.body: A team is a group of people who work together. Read each line with your grown-up. Tick the box next to the one a good team member does.
bullets: ☐ Share your ideas with the team.
☐ Help a friend who is stuck.

explainers.title: 2. Good talking and listening
explainers.body:
Working in a team means talking and listening. Here are the talking-partner rules. Read each one, then tick it after you practise it with a partner.

Now take turns to tell your partner one thing you did yesterday. Did you use all the rules? Give yourself a gold, silver or bronze for your listening today.
bullets: ☐ Look at your partner when you talk.
☐ Listen carefully to what your partner says.
☐ Show you are listening: nod, smile or answer.

explainers.title: 3. What are you good at?
explainers.body:
Everyone is good at something! In the big box, draw a picture of you doing something you are good at. It could be running, drawing, singing, counting or helping.

Now finish these sentences out loud to a partner. Look at them, take turns, and really listen.

explainers.title: 4. Ask your team: a little survey
explainers.body:
A survey is a way to find out what lots of people think. You ask everyone the same question. Ask five people this question: 'Do you like working in a team?' Put a tick in the box for each answer.

Now count your ticks. Did more people say yes or no? Tell your grown-up what you found out.

rows: Yes, I like working in a team
No, I like working on my own

explainers.title: 5. Who makes a building?
explainers.body: It takes lots of people to make a building. Read each job and what they do. Draw a line to match them, or say the answer out loud.

rows: makes sure the building is strong and will not fall down
puts the building together, piece by piece
draws and designs how the building will look
helps everyone listen and do their job

explainers.title: 6. Draw your bridge
explainers.body:
Your team will build a bridge from paper, string and tape. It must be strong enough to hold 10 coins! In the box, draw your idea for a paper bridge. Make it as strong as you can.

Tell your team about your bridge. Use these words: My idea is ... and We could ... Then listen to their ideas too. You can take the best bits of everyone's ideas to make one strong bridge!

Think about what will make your bridge strong. Will you fold the paper? Will you roll it into tubes? Try it and see.

explainers.title: 7. Our team jobs
explainers.body: When your team builds together, everyone needs a job. Write the name of the person in your team next to each job.

rows: Manager — helps everyone listen and take turns
Errand runner — gets the materials the team needs
Recorder — takes photos or notes of the work

explainers.title: 8. A building I like
explainers.body: Think about the buildings where you live, in Hargeisa, Mogadishu, Berbera or your own town. In the box, draw and label a building you like. Give your picture a title at the top.

explainers.title: Before you go
explainers.body:
You have learned so much about teams and buildings! Think back over your activities and answer these out loud with your grown-up.

Well done! You are ready for the big team build. Turn to the Mini-Project & Reflection sheet to design and build your own structure.
bullets: What is one new thing you found out today?
What are you good at that would help a building team?
Why is it good to know what you are good at?

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor (with a grown-up)
lines: With your grown-up, ask your AI tutor to read the four jobs aloud.
Ask it: Which of these jobs would suit me best?
Tell the tutor which job you would like, and why.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor (with a grown-up)
lines: With your grown-up, tell your AI tutor what your team built and why.
Ask it: What is one thing you like about our building idea?
Ask the tutor for one more idea to make our model even better next time.

speakingPrompts.title: Talk about it
lines: Do you like playing games in a team? When is it fun?
Tell your grown-up about a time you worked with someone else.

speakingPrompts.title: Talk about it
lines: Why do you like this building?
If you could build one new building for your town, what would it be?

speakingPrompts.title: Talk about it with your team
lines: Who did you work with in your team?
Can you say one thing each person did that helped?
Was it easier to do this in a team than on your own?
Did you need help during the task? Who did you ask?
What did you enjoy most about working with your team?
Last of all, finish these two sentences out loud or draw the answers. This helps you think about your learning.

teacherSessions.title: Our team promise
lines: We will listen to everyone's ideas.
We will take turns and share the materials.
We will help each other and be kind.
We will keep trying, even if it is tricky.

grownUpGuide.label: For the grown-up
grownUpGuide.intro: This part is written for the parent or teacher sitting with the learner, and is kept in their own words.

sections.title: Before you begin
sections.body:
Hello, and welcome to your child's first Global Perspectives project at Ehel Academy. This guide is written for you, the grown-up. In this subject, children do not memorise long lists of facts. Instead, they gently grow a set of thinking-and-doing skills they will use for the rest of their lives: working together, sharing ideas, speaking and listening, thinking about their own learning, and finding things out. This first project trains those skills through a topic that seven- and eight-year-olds love: building things.

You do not need to be an expert, and you do not need special equipment. You need a warm voice, a little time about twice a week, some paper and boxes, and a willingness to let your child talk, try, and sometimes get it a bit wrong. That is exactly how these skills grow.

sections.title: About this project: We can build it!
sections.body:
Over this unit your child and a small team will work towards one big, exciting goal: to design and build a model of a structure (such as a house, a bridge, a tower or a shop) out of simple, recycled materials. Everything along the way builds up to that final task.

The journey is broken into six short, picture-led lessons, then the final building task, then a gentle reflection. Along the way children play a team game, discover what they are good at, find out who really makes a building, meet the different jobs on a building team, build and test a paper bridge, and dream up a building their own town needs. The topic is the fun part; the real learning is happening quietly underneath it.

sections.title: The skills your child will grow
sections.body:
This project gently grows four Global Perspectives skills. Here they are in plain words, with the questions to listen for:

You will not test these skills or give marks. You simply give children lots of friendly chances to practise them, and you notice out loud when they do them well. A quick 'That was great listening, Amal' teaches more than any worksheet.
items: Working together (collaboration) — taking turns, sharing materials, agreeing on jobs, and helping each other. Listen for: 'Shall we do it this way?' and 'Can I help you?'
Sharing ideas, speaking and listening (communication) — saying an idea clearly, and really listening to a friend's idea. Listen for: 'My idea is ...' and 'What do you think?'
Thinking about our learning (reflection) — stopping to ask how it went and what we would do next time. Listen for: 'That worked well' and 'Next time I would ...'
Finding out (a little research) — looking, asking, and noticing, such as who makes a building or what buildings their town already has.

sections.title: How this unit works at Ehel Academy
sections.body:
Children of this age cannot study on their own, so this unit is led by you, the teacher or parent. Ehel Academy's young model has three parts that work together:

There is no rush and no fixed timetable. Spread the six lessons across two or three weeks, or more. If your child is enjoying the bridge, let them build three bridges. Curiosity is the goal.
items: You, the grown-up, leading the way. You read the lessons aloud, run the simple activities, and keep everything warm and playful. Each lesson is short, about 20 to 40 minutes, and can be split into smaller pieces.

Teacher sessions about twice a week. In these live sessions children play the team games, do the building, and share their ideas with other learners. Much of this project works best with a small group.

A 24-hour AI tutor, used together with a grown-up. The AI tutor can read a lesson aloud, ask your child a simple question, tell a short story, or suggest an activity. At this age the tutor is always used with you sitting alongside, never alone.

sections.title: Meet Rami and his friends
sections.body:
So the lessons feel friendly, we follow a small team of children at Ehel Academy in Hargeisa. Your child can imagine working right alongside them.

Together, Rami, Amal, Karim and Nadia are a little building team. As your child meets each new idea, they will see what Rami's team does with it. Later, your child will do the very same thing with their own team, which can be classmates, brothers and sisters, or friends.
items: Rami loves buildings. He is always drawing towers and bridges and asking how things stand up. He dreams of being an architect one day.
Amal is calm and kind, and she is very good at listening and helping everyone in the team take a turn.
Karim has big ideas and lots of energy. He is learning to slow down and let others speak too.
Nadia is careful and tidy. She likes to keep the plan and remember what the team decided.

sections.title: How to run the six short lessons
sections.body: Each lesson has the same simple shape: a short Aim (what it is for), a Talk about prompt (to get children thinking and speaking), and a Do activity (the hands-on part). Read the Aim to yourself, then use the Talk about and Do parts with your child. Keep it light. Lots of talking is exactly right.

sections.title: Lesson 1.1 - How do we work together?
sections.body:
Aim. Children begin to feel what good teamwork looks like, and meet the word team.

Talk about. Ask: 'Do you like playing games in a team? When is it fun? When is it hard?' Let your child tell a story about a time they played or worked with others.

Do. Play one quick team game together, such as a simple 'Capture the Castle' or any game where a team must cooperate to win. Then play the good-team sorting game: read each pair below and let your child choose which one makes a good team member.

The good-team choice is always the first one. Finish with a quick family or class survey: ask everyone 'Do you like playing games in teams?' and count the answers. This quietly introduces the idea that a survey means asking lots of people the same question.
items: Share your ideas with the team — or — let other people give all the ideas?
Listen to other people's ideas — or — only think about your own?
Put the best bits of everyone's ideas together — or — use only your own idea?
The whole team decides together — or — only the cleverest person decides?
Help others in your group — or — only do your own bit?
If you are stuck, ask for help — or — stay stuck and say nothing?

sections.title: Lesson 1.2 - What are you good at?
sections.body:
Aim. Children notice what they are good at and enjoy, and practise good talking and listening with a partner.

Talk about. Look at people who do different jobs to make a film: a camera operator, a sound engineer, an actor and a director. Ask: 'What do you think each person is good at?' Then ask your child: 'What are you good at? What do you enjoy?'

Do. Teach the talking-partners rules and practise them while your child tells a partner (you, a sibling or a friend) one thing they are good at:

Afterwards, let your child rate how well they talked and listened today: gold, silver or bronze. Gently point out one thing they did well.
items: Sit facing your partner.
Take turns to speak.
Look at your partner when you talk.
Listen to what your partner says.
Show you are interested by nodding, smiling or answering.

sections.title: Lesson 1.3 - Who makes a building?
sections.body:
Aim. Children find out that people work together to make a building: an architect designs it, and an engineer makes sure it stands up.

Talk about. Picture a big city with tall buildings. Ask: 'What can you see? Is it the same as or different from where we live? Who do you think made all this?'

Do. Share this true, wow-worthy fact: in the city of Dubai, people built the tallest building in the whole world, called the Burj Khalifa. People came from all over the globe to help. Then read the two little messages below and ask who did which job:

sections.title: Lesson 1.4 - Who else works on a new building?
sections.body:
Aim. Children discover that a building needs many people with different jobs, and they meet the four team roles used later in the project.

Talk about. Ask: 'Which building job would you like best? Why? What are you good at that would help?'

Do. If you have a small group, play find your team: give each child a role card, and let them walk around asking others 'What do you do?' until they gather a team with different jobs. Then meet the four roles:

Read out the team's first challenge so children can start thinking about it: 'In your group, you will make a bridge using only paper, string and sticky tape. Your bridge must hold the weight of 10 coins.' Ask which role each child would like for that task, and why.
items: Manager — helps everyone listen to each other and stay on task.
Errand runner — lists the materials the team needs, fetches them, and takes questions to the teacher.
Recorder and presenter — takes photos or notes, and later tells the class what the team did.
Builder — follows the team's plan and puts the structure together.

sections.title: Lesson 1.5 - What's your idea?
sections.body:
Aim. Children share ideas, decide together, and build and test a paper bridge as a team. This is the big practice run before the final task.

Talk about. Ask: 'What kinds of bridges do you know? What could a bridge made of paper look like?' Let your child draw one idea for a paper bridge.

Do. Sort out a fairness problem first: in one team, everyone wanted to be the builder and nobody wanted to manage. Ask your child: 'What could they do to decide fairly?' (Take turns, swap jobs, or vote.) Then help your child's team choose roles and build their bridge, following this simple checklist:

It does not matter if the bridge sags or the tower leans. A wobble is a wonderful learning moment: ask 'What could we change to make it stronger?' At the end, let each child colour in some stars to show how helpful they were to the team today.
items: Listen to everyone's ideas.
Vote for the best idea, or take the best bits of several ideas.
Make a list of the materials you need.
Build the bridge.
Take photos or notes as you work.
Test your bridge with 10 coins!

sections.title: Lesson 1.6 - What would we like to build where we live?
sections.body:
Aim. Children look at their own town and imagine a building it needs. This links the wider world back to home.

Talk about. Ask: 'What buildings do you like in our town or region? Tell me about one.' Talk about the buildings families use together, such as a school, a hospital, a market, a library, a mosque or a church.

Do. Play a quick game of I-Spy with buildings you can see or remember. Then let your child draw and label a building they like, give the picture a title, and describe it to you. Finally, invite them to imagine they are a developer: 'If you could build one new building for our town, what would it be, and why?' Share ideas warmly, taking turns and using kind words like 'That is a great idea!' and 'What a good suggestion!'

sections.title: Key words for this unit
sections.body: These are the words children meet in this project. Say them often and warmly. There is no need to test them.

rows: A group of people who work together.
Doing something with other people, not on your own.
To give some of what you have, like sharing your ideas or your materials.
A thought about what to do or make.
To hear carefully what someone else is saying.
Thinking about what you will do before you do it.
To draw or plan how something will look before you make it.
To make something by putting parts together.
Something that has been built, like a house, a bridge or a tower.
A person who makes sure a building is strong and safe.
A person who puts the building together.
The team member who helps everyone listen and stay on task.
The things you build with, like paper, boxes, string or tape.
A structure that lets you cross over something, like water or a road.
A way to find out what lots of people think by asking them the same question.

sections.title: What you will need
sections.body: Nothing fancy. Save these over a week or two before you start, and keep them in a box:
items: Paper and scrap paper, plus crayons or coloured pencils.
String and sticky tape (or glue).
About 10 coins, or small stones, to test the bridge.
Recycled materials for the final model: cardboard boxes, tubes, plastic bottles, bottle tops, old fabric, lids.
A phone or notebook to take photos or notes of the work (optional but lovely).
The Activity Sheet and the Mini-Project & Reflection sheet from this unit.

sections.title: Using the AI tutor together
sections.body:
At this age, the AI tutor is a helper you use side by side with your child, never a babysitter. Sit together, and let the tutor do the things a patient helper does well:

Whenever you see an Ask Your AI Tutor (with a grown-up) box in the children's sheets, that is your cue to open the tutor together. Keep sessions short and cheerful, and always stay in the room. If the tutor suggests something you would rather not do, simply skip it; you are in charge.
items: Read aloud. Ask it to read a lesson, a checklist or a story slowly, so your child can follow.
Ask simple questions. Ask it to ask your child one friendly question, then let your child answer out loud.
Tell a short story. Ask for a two-minute story about a team that built something together.
Suggest an activity. Ask it for one easy idea to try with the materials you have at home.

sections.title: The Final task: design and build a structure
sections.body:
Everything leads to this. In a team of a few children, your child will agree on a building their town or region needs, decide who does which job, and then design and build a model of it from recycled materials. Finally, the team presents their model and tells everyone what it is, why they chose it, and what it is made of.

The full, child-friendly steps are in the separate Mini-Project & Reflection sheet. Your role is to gather the materials, keep the team kind and fair, and help only when they are truly stuck. Remember that a wobbly, hand-made model that the children are proud of is a complete success.

sections.title: Thinking about our work: a simple reflection
sections.body:
To finish, help the team look back and ask 'How successful was our building task?' Keep it gentle and spoken. The Mini-Project & Reflection sheet has a picture checklist with happy and not-yet faces, some stars to colour, and a few talking questions such as:

This looking-back is a real Global Perspectives skill (reflection), and it matters as much as the building. When children hear that their thinking and teamwork are valued, not just the finished model, they learn the lesson that lasts.
items: Who did you work with in your team?
Can you say one thing each person did that helped?
Was it easier to do this task in a team than on your own?
Did you need help during the task? Who did you ask?
What did you enjoy most about working with your team?

sections.title: Keeping it warm and fun
sections.body: You now have everything you need. Go at your child's pace, celebrate the wobbles as much as the wins, and talk far more than you worry about getting it 'right'. If your child finishes this unit believing that they can share an idea, listen to a friend, and build something together, then the project has done its job beautifully. Have fun building it, together.

project.title: Mini-project
project.intro: This is the big one! At Ehel Academy, Rami and his friends built a model together, and now it is your turn. With your team and a grown-up, you are going to design and build a model of a structure for your town. Then you will look back and think about how your team did. Take your time, share the jobs, and be kind to each other.

steps.title: Choose what to build
steps.intro:
Talk together and agree on one building your town or region really needs. Here are some ideas to help you choose:

You could pick one of these, or think of your own. Talk about where in your town you would build it, and why your town needs it. When your team agrees, fill in this plan together.
items: a school or a library
a hospital or a clinic
a shop, a market or a supermarket
a bridge, a tower or a lighthouse for the port at Berbera
a place where people gather, like a mosque or a church
a police station, a post office or a theatre

steps.title: Choose your team jobs
steps.intro: Every person needs a job. Decide together who will do each one. If lots of you want the same job, take turns or have a quick vote.

rows: Helps everyone listen and stay on task.
Draws the plan of how the building will look.
Makes the model from the materials.
Fetches the materials and asks the teacher questions.
Takes photos or notes, and tells the class about it.

steps.title: Gather your materials
steps.intro: Use recycled materials you have saved. With your errand runner, make a list of what you need, then collect it. You might use:
items: cardboard boxes and tubes
plastic bottles, lids and bottle tops
paper, string, sticky tape and glue
old fabric or newspaper

steps.title: Draw your plan
steps.intro: Before you build, your designer draws a plan. In the box, draw your building and label the parts. This is your team's design.

steps.title: Build your model
steps.intro:
Now build it together! Your builder puts the pieces together, and everyone helps. Use these top tips to help your team work well:

Your recorder can take photos or make notes while you work. Do not worry if a part falls down or looks wobbly. That happens to real builders too! Just talk about it and try a new way.
items: Listen to everyone's ideas.
Share the materials and take turns.
Follow your plan, but you can change it to make it better.
Be a kind team member and help each other.
If you are stuck, ask your teacher or grown-up.

steps.title: Check and test your model
steps.intro: Look at your model together. Does it stand up on its own? Is it strong? Gently test it. If a part is weak, add more tape or a stronger piece and try again. Fixing your model is part of being a good builder.

steps.title: Show your model to everyone
steps.intro: When your model is ready, show it to the class or your family. Your recorder can help. Tell everyone:
items: what you have built
why you chose it
where you would build it in your town
what your model is made of
what the real building would be made of

reflection.prompt: The thing I am most proud of is ...

assessment.note: Stages 1-3 are assessed through the mini-project and the look-back grid; the source pack ships no quiz.

selfAssessment.statement: Our model shows a building our town would like.
We all had a job to do, and we did it.
Everyone in our team shared an idea.
We took turns and listened to each other.
